question: Abram casts [Lightning Bolt] targeting Nola. As it resolves, can Abram choose to deal the damage to Nola's [Vivien Reid]?
gold: No. Lightning Bolt deals damage to its target, Nola. There is no rule that allows damage dealt to a player to be redirected to a planeswalker.
opus_answer:
No. Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to Nola, and Abram cannot switch that damage to Nola's Vivien Reid on resolution.

Two reasons:

1. The old planeswalker redirection rule no longer exists. Under the current rules, a player can no longer choose to have noncombat damage that would be dealt to an opponent be dealt to a planeswalker that opponent controls instead; that rule was removed, and cards that still do this were given Oracle errata to deal damage directly to planeswalkers [306.7]. Lightning Bolt's text is simply "Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to any target," with no redirection clause.

2. The target is locked in when the spell is cast, not chosen at resolution. Lightning Bolt says "any target," which may be a creature, player, planeswalker, or battle [115.4]. Abram chose Nola as that target when casting, and only an effect that specifically changes targets or chooses new targets can alter it [115.7b]. Redirection effects (a kind of replacement effect that moves damage from one creature, planeswalker, or player to another) exist, but only if some spell or ability actually creates one, such as a card that says the next X damage to one target is dealt to another target instead [614.9, Redirection Effect]. Neither Lightning Bolt nor Vivien Reid provides such an effect.

If Abram wants to damage Vivien Reid, he must target Vivien Reid with Lightning Bolt in the first place, which rule 115.4 permits since planeswalkers are legal choices for "any target."

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more than two; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Addison casts [Ferocious Zheng]. After it resolves, they cast [Elemental Eruption] and reveal [Everdream] from their hand, splicing it onto Elemental Eruption. When Elemental Eruption's Storm trigger resolves, will the copies of Elemental Eruption also have Everdream spliced onto them?
gold: Yes. As Addison is casting Elemental Eruption they choose whether they want to splice as part of the casting process. When the storm trigger resolves it copies all the choices made when casting the original spell, including the choice to splice.
opus_answer:
Yes. The copy of Elemental Eruption created by its storm ability will have Everdream's text spliced onto it, so it also draws Addison a card.

Why: splicing is a choice made while casting Elemental Eruption, and copying a spell copies both its characteristics and all decisions made for it [707.10]. Everdream's own ruling states this directly: "If a spell is copied, choices made while casting it are copied, so the copy will have the same abilities spliced onto it as the original" [Everdream ruling #4]. Splice works by adding Everdream's rules text to Elemental Eruption as a text-changing effect [702.47c, 612.10], and that added text resolves after Elemental Eruption's own effect [Everdream ruling #1, 702.47b].

Storm count here: storm copies the spell for each other spell cast before it this turn [702.40a]. Ferocious Zheng was cast this turn, so there's exactly 1 copy. Revealing and paying for Everdream via splice is not casting Everdream, so it does not add to the storm count. Net result: Elemental Eruption plus one copy resolve, creating two 4/4 red Dragon Elemental tokens with flying and prowess and drawing two cards total.

A couple of notes: the copy is put directly onto the stack and isn't cast, so it won't be counted by later storm spells [Elemental Eruption ruling #2, 707.10]. The copy is also still a red sorcery — splice doesn't give it Everdream's name, mana cost, or color [702.47c]. The storm copy resolves before the original Elemental Eruption, since copies go on the stack above it [608.1].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players — storm counts all spells cast by any player this turn, and the splice-copying rule is unaffected by player count.

gpt_answer: Yes. Each copy created by Elemental Eruption’s storm will also have Everdream spliced onto it, assuming Everdream was properly revealed and its splice cost was paid when Elemental Eruption was cast. Reasoning: “Splice” is a text-changing effect that adds the spliced card’s rules text to the spell on the stack (see rule [702.47c] and [612.10]). A copy of a spell copies the characteristics of the original spell and all decisions made while casting it, including additional effects added by splice (see rule [707.10]). The Everdream ruling explicitly confirms that if a spell is copied, choices made while casting it are copied and “the copy will have the same abilities spliced onto it as the original” ([Everdream ruling #4]). Elemental Eruption’s copies are put directly onto the stack and aren’t cast, but they still copy the original spell’s characteristics and the splice choices ([Elemental Eruption ruling #2]; [707.10]). Also note you must have revealed all cards you intend to splice when casting the spell ([Everdream ruling #5]).

question: Nylah controls [Alpine Moon] choosing "[Vesuva]". Adrien plays Vesuva choosing [Urban Retreat] as it enters. Does it enter the battlefield tapped or untapped?
gold: This can't happen as described. Adrien cannot choose a land to copy with Vesuva because it loses that ability before it would apply. Vesuva enters untapped, as itself.
opus_answer:
It enters the battlefield tapped.

Why: Vesuva's ability is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters — "You may have this land enter tapped as a copy of any land on the battlefield." When several replacement effects want to modify the same enters-the-battlefield event, and one of them would make the object a copy of something, that copy effect must be chosen and applied first [616.1c], [616.1f]. So Adrien applies Vesuva's copy effect first: Vesuva enters as a copy of Urban Retreat, which means it also copies Urban Retreat's name and its printed ability "This land enters tapped" [707.5], [Vesuva ruling #0], [Vesuva ruling #3].

Now you re-check which other replacement effects apply, using the permanent's characteristics as it would exist on the battlefield after the effects already applied [614.12]. At that point the land's name is Urban Retreat, not Vesuva, so Nylah's Alpine Moon — which only affects "lands your opponents control with the chosen name" (Vesuva) — simply doesn't apply to it. Alpine Moon never strips the "enters tapped" ability, so both Vesuva's own "enter tapped" clause and the copied Urban Retreat ability leave it tapped.

Contrast: if Adrien's Vesuva were entering without copying anything (no land chosen), it would still be named Vesuva, Alpine Moon would apply and strip its land types and abilities, and it would enter untapped as a land that only has "{T}: Add one mana of any color" [Alpine Moon ruling #0], [Vesuva ruling #2].

Assumption: Adrien is an opponent of Nylah's (Alpine Moon only affects opponents' lands). This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — the only thing that changes with more players is that simultaneous choices are made in APNAP order [101.4].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
gpt_answer:
Vesuva enters the battlefield untapped. Alpine Moon (naming “Vesuva”) causes lands your opponents control named Vesuva to lose abilities that would make them enter tapped before those abilities can apply, so Vesuva can’t use an “enter tapped” option when copying Urban Retreat.

Reasoning: Vesuva’s copying process would normally copy “This land enters tapped.” from Urban Retreat (see Vesuva ruling #0 and rule [707.5]), which would let Vesuva enter tapped if its controller chose that. However, Alpine Moon’s effect (already on the battlefield) makes lands named Vesuva lose abilities, and Alpine Moon ruling #0 specifically says an affected land’s ability that causes it to enter the battlefield tapped is lost before it applies. Rule [614.12] directs you to take continuous effects that already exist (like Alpine Moon) into account when determining how a permanent enters the battlefield, so Alpine Moon removes the entering-tapped ability before Vesuva’s “enter tapped as a copy” can take effect. Therefore Vesuva enters untapped as it copies Urban Retreat.

question: Ares controls [Mycosynth Lattice] and casts [Glittering Wish]. Are they able to choose a card?
gold: Yes, Ares may choose any multicolored card. Cards outside the game are not affected by Mycosynth Lattice.
opus_answer:
Yes — Ares can still choose a multicolored card with Glittering Wish.

Why: Mycosynth Lattice's second ability says "All cards that aren't on the battlefield, spells, and permanents are colorless," and its ruling clarifies that this makes everything colorless "in every zone of the game" [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2]. Cards outside the game — such as those in Ares's sideboard — are not in any of the game's zones; outside the game is not a zone at all [400.11a], and sideboard cards are outside the game [400.11a, 100.4]. So Mycosynth Lattice's color-changing effect doesn't reach them, and a multicolored card in Ares's sideboard is still multicolored when Glittering Wish resolves and asks him to reveal "a multicolored card you own from outside the game."

Once that card is revealed and put into Ares's hand, it is then in a game zone and Mycosynth Lattice makes it colorless from that point on — but that happens after the choice, so it doesn't stop Glittering Wish from finding it.

Note also that Glittering Wish says "may," so Ares is never forced to find one, and searching/finding from outside the game is a matter of choosing an appropriate card he owns [701.23j].

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Does [Gemini Engine]'s token enter the battlefield tapped?
gold: No.
opus_answer:
No. The Twin token created by Gemini Engine enters the battlefield untapped, and attacking. Gemini Engine's ability says only that the token is created "attacking" — it says nothing about the token being tapped, and a token has no characteristics or status other than what the creating ability defines [111.3]. Permanents enter the battlefield untapped, unflipped, face up, and phased in unless a spell or ability says otherwise [110.5b], and Gemini Engine doesn't say otherwise. This is confirmed directly by the ruling: "The Twin token enters as an untapped attacking creature. It's not subject to any costs to attack or restrictions on attacking" [Gemini Engine ruling #3].

Note that attacking and being tapped are separate things — creatures are normally tapped as a cost of being declared as attackers, but a token put onto the battlefield already attacking skips the declare-attackers process entirely, so it is never tapped. This means the Twin can still be tapped later for an effect that requires tapping an untapped creature.

One caveat: an outside effect such as a permanent that reads "Permanents enter tapped" would be a replacement effect modifying how the token enters [614.1c], [614.12], and would make the Twin enter tapped; also, since a replacement effect applying to a token entering the battlefield is applied after continuous effects that modify its characteristics [701.7b]. Absent such an effect, the Twin is untapped. This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more than two; Gemini Engine's ability affects only its controller's own token.

question: Carolyn is the monarch. Alexis cast [Palace Jailer]. When it enters the battlefield, Alexis target Baylor's [Skull Prophet] with the second ability. Carolyn counters the first triggered ability with [Consign to Memory]. After everything resolves, Alexis pass the turn. On Baylor's turn they deal combat damage to Carolyn. Will Skull Prophet return from exile?
gold: Yes. When Palace Jailer's second triggered ability resolves it has a duration that expires when the monarch changes to an opponent.
opus_answer:
Yes — Skull Prophet returns to the battlefield when Baylor becomes the monarch by dealing combat damage to Carolyn.

Why: Because Consign to Memory countered Palace Jailer's first triggered ability, Alexis never became the monarch; Carolyn stayed the monarch. Per [Palace Jailer ruling #6], when Palace Jailer's second ability resolves while its controller (Alexis) is not the monarch, Skull Prophet is exiled until there is a *new* monarch and that new monarch is one of Alexis's opponents — Carolyn already being the monarch does not immediately bring Skull Prophet back.

Being the monarch carries the inherent triggered ability "Whenever a creature deals combat damage to the monarch, its controller becomes the monarch" [725.2], [Palace Jailer ruling #1]. So when Baylor's creature deals combat damage to Carolyn, Baylor becomes the monarch. Baylor is an opponent of Alexis, which satisfies the exile duration; it does not matter that Baylor is also the exiled card's owner — any opponent becoming the monarch causes the return [Palace Jailer ruling #5]. The one-shot exile effect "until" that event ends, and a second one-shot effect immediately returns the card to the battlefield under its owner's control, i.e., Baylor's [610.3c].

Notes: this scenario is inherently multiplayer (Alexis, Baylor, Carolyn), and the monarch rules used here apply the same regardless of player count; with only two players there'd simply be no third player to hold the monarchy. Also, Palace Jailer leaving the battlefield would not bring Skull Prophet back — the game keeps watching for the next time an opponent becomes the monarch [Palace Jailer ruling #3].

gpt_answer:
Yes. Skull Prophet will return to the battlefield when Baylor becomes the monarch.

Why: Palace Jailer’s second triggered ability exiled Skull Prophet “until an opponent becomes the monarch,” so the exile is an “until” one-shot effect that will be ended by the specified event and then return the object to the battlefield under its owner’s control [610.3c]. Consign to Memory countering Palace Jailer’s first triggered ability only prevented Alexis from becoming the monarch at that time; Palace Jailer’s second ability still exiled Skull Prophet and is waiting for “an opponent” to become the monarch [Palace Jailer ruling #6]. The game rule that makes a player the monarch when a creature deals combat damage to the monarch (“Whenever a creature deals combat damage to the monarch, its controller becomes the monarch”) means Baylor becomes the monarch when Baylor’s creature deals combat damage to Carolyn [725.2]. Palace Jailer’s official ruling confirms that any opponent becoming the monarch (not necessarily the creature’s former controller) will cause the exiled card to return [Palace Jailer ruling #5]. Therefore, when Baylor becomes the monarch as a result of dealing combat damage to Carolyn, Skull Prophet returns to the battlefield under its owner’s control [610.3c; Palace Jailer ruling #5].

Assumption on timing: I assumed the combat damage and the resulting monarch change happen after Palace Jailer’s exile ability resolved and while Skull Prophet is still exiled. If Baylor had already been the monarch at the moment Palace Jailer’s exile ability resolved, the exile would still persist until “an opponent becomes the monarch” again per Palace Jailer’s ruling [Palace Jailer ruling #6].

question: Addison casts [Touch of the Void] targeting Nova's [Orzhov Racketeers]. Does Nova still get spirit tokens?
gold: No. A creature is considered to have "died" if it moves from the battlefield to the graveyard.. Touch of the Void replaces the creature moving to the graveyard with moving the creature to exile instead, which doesn't qualify as the creature dying, and therefore doesn't cause the afterlife. Trigger to go onto the stack. ([702.135a])
opus_answer:
No — Nova gets no Spirit tokens. Touch of the Void's replacement effect says that if a creature dealt damage this way would die this turn, it's exiled instead. Orzhov Racketeers is a 3/2, so 3 damage is lethal and it would be destroyed as a state-based action, but instead of going to the graveyard it goes to exile. Afterlife 2 only triggers when Orzhov Racketeers dies (is put into a graveyard from the battlefield); since that never happens, the afterlife ability never triggers and no 1/1 white and black Spirit tokens are created.

Note the replacement lasts the whole turn, not just for the damage itself: per Touch of the Void ruling #4, once Orzhov Racketeers has been dealt damage by Touch of the Void, if it would die for any reason later that turn (another burn spell, a -X/-X effect, a sacrifice-free destruction, etc.), it's exiled instead — so afterlife stays shut off for the rest of the turn. If Orzhov Racketeers somehow leaves the battlefield and returns, it's a new object with no memory of its previous existence (rule 400.7), so the exile-replacement no longer applies to it and afterlife could work normally.

One timing caveat: this assumes Touch of the Void's damage is what causes Orzhov Racketeers to die. If Orzhov Racketeers had already been put into a graveyard before Touch of the Void resolved, afterlife would already have triggered and the tokens would be created. This answer doesn't depend on the number of players at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
gpt_answer:
No. Nova won’t get Spirit tokens because Orzhov Racketeers is exiled instead of dying, so its Afterlife ability never triggers.

Reasoning: Touch of the Void deals 3 damage and, per Touch of the Void ruling #4, “after being dealt damage, if [a creature] would die for any reason that turn, it’ll be exiled instead.” That means Orzhov Racketeers is moved to exile rather than being put into its owner’s graveyard. The Afterlife ability on Orzhov Racketeers is a zone-change (“dies”) trigger; such triggers are checked by looking back to see whether the zone-change event that matches the trigger actually occurred. Because Orzhov Racketeers changed zones to exile instead of to the graveyard, the “dies” event did not occur and Orzhov Racketeers’ Afterlife 2 ability does not trigger, so Nova does not receive any Spirit tokens.

question: Abdullah controls [Liquimetal Coating], [Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker], and [Karn, the Great Creator]. Abdullah uses Liquimetal Coating to make Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker into an artifact, then uses Karn, the Great Creator's first ability to turn Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker into a creature and passes the turn. Natalie then attacks Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker with [Walking Corpse]. Can Abdullah block with Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker? If so, what happens?
gold:
Yes, any creature controlled by the defending player can block an attacker. Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker will be dealt 2 damage, resulting in 2 damage being marked on it and it losing two loyalty counters.

Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker is still a planeswalker. Effects that make a permanent an 'artifact creature' allow that permanent to retain its other types. Damage dealt to Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker will still result in loyalty counters being removed from it.

Yes — Abdullah can block Walking Corpse with Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker, provided Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker is untapped.

Why: only creatures can block, and after Liquimetal Coating and Karn, the Great Creator's +1 ability, Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker is an artifact creature (with power and toughness each equal to its mana value, 8, so an 8/8) that is still also a planeswalker [506.3, 302.5]. When declaring blockers, Abdullah chooses untapped creatures he controls that aren't battles, and each may block a creature that's attacking Abdullah, a planeswalker Abdullah controls, or a battle Abdullah protects [509.1, 509.1a]. Walking Corpse is attacking Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker, which is a planeswalker Abdullah controls, so Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker legally blocks the very creature attacking it.

After the block, Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker is simultaneously a blocking creature and a planeswalker that's being attacked. It stays in combat in both roles; it would only be removed from combat entirely if it stopped being both a creature and a planeswalker. If it stops being just one of those types (for example, Karn, the Great Creator's animation ending), it continues in the other role — still a blocking creature, or still a planeswalker being attacked, whichever applies [506.4d]. Note also that Karn, the Great Creator's +1 required a *noncreature* artifact as its target, which is why the Liquimetal Coating activation had to come first.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Liquimetal Coating resolved before Karn, the Great Creator's +1 was activated (as stated) and that both effects are still in place when blockers are declared. If the animation from Karn, the Great Creator had already ended before the declare blockers step, Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker would be a noncreature permanent and could not block at all [506.3].

On the combat damage itself: the rules supplied here cover legality of the block, not how combat damage is dealt to a permanent that is both a creature and a planeswalker, so I won't state loyalty-versus-damage specifics — that portion isn't in the provided context.

Multiplayer: with more than two players, the same answer holds; each defending player declares blockers in APNAP order and may block only creatures attacking that player, a planeswalker they control, or a battle they protect [802.4a, 101.4]. Under the shared team turns option the defending team makes one combined legal block instead [805.10d].

gpt_answer:
Yes. Abdullah can block with Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker. Karn, the Great Creator’s +1 made Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker into an artifact creature with power and toughness equal to its mana value (8/8), so Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker is a creature Abdullah controls and may be chosen as a blocker (see rule 509.1a; only a creature can block per rule 506.3). When Abdullah declares Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker as a blocking creature against Walking Corpse, Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker becomes a blocking creature (see the “Blocking Creature” definition). In the resulting combat interaction Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker will have power and toughness equal to its mana value (8/8) due to Karn, the Great Creator’s effect and Walking Corpse is a 2/2; they will assign and deal combat damage to each other (Walking Corpse deals 2, Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker deals 8).

question: Adrian casts [Opportunistic Dragon] and uses its triggered ability to take control of Natalia's [Volunteer Militia]. Afterwards Adrian uses [Oko, Thief of Crowns]' +1 ability to make Volunteer Militia a 3/3 Elk with no abilities. Will Adrian then be able to attack with Volunteer Militia?

Oko, Thief of Crowns' +1 only overwrites abilities, colors, types, and P/T; effects that add or remove abilities are a distinct thing from restriction effects [113.10, 113.10b]. The card ruling confirms the restriction sticks even through later control changes [Opportunistic Dragon ruling #0].

2. Even ignoring that, Adrian gained control of Volunteer Militia this turn, so on the turn it was stolen it also couldn't attack under the summoning sickness rule — a creature can't attack unless it has been under its controller's control continuously since that player's most recent turn began [302.6], and Volunteer Militia has no haste [702.10b]. The restriction lasts for as long as Opportunistic Dragon remains on the battlefield [611.2b]. This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; nothing here depends on the number of players, other than that Opportunistic Dragon's trigger targets a Human or artifact an opponent controls.

question: Amber has 2 life and attacks with [Drogskol Reaver] and [Gavony Ironwright]. How much damage will be dealt to Neil in total?

4. Regular combat damage step: Drogskol Reaver deals 3 (its now-unbuffed power) and Gavony Ironwright deals 1, for 4 more damage to Neil [510.1a].

4 + 3 + 1 = 8 damage dealt to Neil. Amber ends up gaining 4 (first strike) + 3 (regular) = 7 life total from lifelink, drawing a card for each of those two life-gain events [Drogskol Reaver ruling #1].

If instead either attacker were blocked, that creature's damage would go to the blocking creature(s) rather than to Neil, so less (or no) damage would reach Neil [510.1c]. question: Adonis controls [Tocatli Honor Guard] and [Selvala, Heart of the Wilds]. Adonis casts [Catacomb Slug]. When it enters the battlefield, will Selvala, Heart of the Wilds's ability trigger?

That printed text overrides the general enters-the-battlefield trigger rule (603.6a), and it shuts off not just the entering creature's own ETB triggers but any triggered ability that would trigger on a creature entering — including Selvala, Heart of the Wilds's "Whenever another creature enters" ability [Tocatli Honor Guard ruling #1].

A couple of secondary points:
- Even without Tocatli Honor Guard, Selvala, Heart of the Wilds's ability only lets you draw if the entering creature's power is greater than each other creature's power; Catacomb Slug is 2/6, and Selvala, Heart of the Wilds is 2/3, so the power condition would fail anyway. - Static "as this enters" / "enters tapped" effects are not triggered abilities (603.6d, 614.1c), so Tocatli Honor Guard would not stop those.

This answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table: Tocatli Honor Guard's ability isn't limited to its controller's creatures, so no player's creature entering causes abilities to trigger while it's on the battlefield.

question: Aubriella controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], a [Sapseep Forest], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Sapseep Forest and Saproling look like?
gold:
Applying Life and Limb's effect first would allow Blood Moon's effect to apply to the Saproling, and applying Blood Moon's effect first would prevent Life and Limb from applying to the Sapseep Forest, so both effects are dependent on each other and those dependencies are ignored. Life and Limb has the earlier timestamp, so it's applied first.

As Life and Limb's effect is applied, Sapseep Forest becomes a creature and the Saproling becomes a land. Then as Blood Moon's effect is applied, they both lose their other land types and abilities and becomes Mountains.

Both permanents are 1/1 Green Land Creature - Mountain Saprolings, with "{T}: Add {R}".

Short answer: Sapseep Forest ends up as a noncreature nonbasic land — Mountain that taps for {R}, and the Saproling token ends up as a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also a land — Mountain (not a Forest) with "{T}: Add {R}," and it's subject to summoning sickness.

Why:

All three continuous effects are type-changing effects applied in layer 4 [613.1d], with Life and Limb's timestamp before Blood Moon's [613.7]. Dependency can override timestamps [613.8].

Sapseep Forest: Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") applies to Sapseep Forest no matter what Life and Limb does, while Life and Limb only applies to Forests and Saprolings — so whether Life and Limb applies to Sapseep Forest depends on Blood Moon's result. Blood Moon is applied first: setting a nonbasic land's subtype to a basic land type strips its old land types, its rules-text abilities, and copiable effects affecting it, and gives it "{T}: Add {R}" [305.7, Blood Moon ruling #2]. So Sapseep Forest loses the Forest type, loses "This land enters tapped" and the {G}, {T} life-gain ability, and gains "{T}: Add {R}." Because it is then neither a Forest nor a Saproling, Life and Limb does nothing to it — it stays a noncreature land, Land — Mountain.

The Saproling token: Life and Limb makes it a 1/1 green Saproling creature and a Forest land in addition to its other types [Life and Limb ruling #3, 205.1b]. That makes it a nonbasic land, so Blood Moon then applies to it and sets its land subtype to Mountain, stripping the Forest type and giving it "{T}: Add {R}" instead of "{T}: Add {G}" [305.7, Blood Moon ruling #2]. Setting a land's subtype doesn't remove card types or non-land subtypes, so it keeps the creature type Saproling and the creature card type [305.7, 205.1b]. Result: a 1/1 green Saproling creature land — Mountain. Since you haven't controlled it as a creature since your turn began, you can't pay the {T} of its mana ability [Life and Limb ruling #0].

Assumption on ordering: for the token the two effects arguably each change what the other applies to; I've resolved that by timestamp (Life and Limb first, then Blood Moon) [613.7, 613.8]. The full text of the dependency rule 613.8 wasn't provided here, so if a dependency were judged to exist in the other direction for the token, Blood Moon would be applied before the token was a land and the token would remain a 1/1 green Saproling creature Forest land tapping for {G}.

question: Alonso casts [Piracy] and would like to tap all of Nico's lands but not cast any spells. Can Alonso do this?

Two practical points: (1) The mana produced is restricted by Piracy's own text — it can be spent only to cast spells — so if Alonso casts nothing, that mana just goes unused. (2) The provided rules don't include the rule on when mana pools empty or the general rule permitting mana-ability activation with priority, so I can't cite chapter and verse for those; but nothing here penalizes a player for unspent mana, and no rule provided prevents tapping without a spell.

Multiplayer note: Piracy refers to "lands you don't control," so at a table with more than two players Alonso could tap any opponent's lands, not just Nico's; with exactly two players it's just Nico's. The provided rules contain nothing that changes the answer based on player count.

But the second sentence is not limited to opponents: "Then destroy each artifact with mana value less than or equal to the number of rust counters on it." Mox Tantalite has mana value 0, and the number of rust counters on it is 0. Since 0 is less than or equal to 0, it meets the condition and is destroyed, and Corrosion specifies it can't be regenerated. [Corrosion ruling #2] confirms Corrosion "destroys all artifacts with rust counters on them, even your own" — the key point being that the destruction clause reaches your own artifacts, not just the targeted opponent's. Mox Tantalite's mana value of 0 is what makes it die immediately even without ever receiving a counter.

Timing/state caveat: if Mox Tantalite is still exiled with suspend time counters, it isn't a permanent at all and can't be destroyed — cards not on the battlefield have no permanent status ([110.5d]). Only once it has been cast off suspend and is on the battlefield does Corrosion's trigger see it.

Two players vs. multiplayer: this doesn't change. Corrosion targets one opponent for the rust-counter part, so in a multiplayer game only that chosen opponent's artifacts get counters; but the destruction clause checks every artifact on the battlefield regardless of controller, so Aisha's Mox Tantalite dies either way ([Corrosion ruling #1], [Corrosion ruling #2]).

question: Adalynn attacks Nico with [Mass of Ghouls]. Nico declares no blockers but casts [Gideon's Sacrifice] to cause their [Stormwild Capridor] to take five damage instead of them. What will happen when the damage occurs?

Stormwild Capridor is dealt all 5 combat damage from Mass of Ghouls and is destroyed. Its prevention ability doesn't help.

Why: Gideon's Sacrifice is a redirection effect "" a replacement effect that causes damage that would be dealt to Nico and permanents Nico controls to be dealt to the chosen permanent, Stormwild Capridor, instead (see rule 614.9 and the Redirection Effect glossary entry). Crucially, Gideon's Sacrifice doesn't change the source of the damage or whether the damage is combat damage [Gideon's Sacrifice ruling #3]. Mass of Ghouls's 5 damage is still combat damage dealt by Mass of Ghouls. Stormwild Capridor's ability only reads "If noncombat damage would be dealt to this creature, prevent that damage" "" it does nothing against combat damage, so no damage is prevented and no +1/+1 counters are put on it [Stormwild Capridor ruling #1].

More damage may be redirected to Stormwild Capridor than it has toughness [Gideon's Sacrifice ruling #1], so all 5 damage lands on the 1/3 Stormwild Capridor at once. That damage stays marked on it, and since 5 is greater than or equal to its toughness of 3, it has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed the next time state-based actions are checked (rule 120.6). Nico takes no damage.

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with more than two players "" Mass of Ghouls is attacking Nico specifically, and the redirection only involves Nico's own permanent.

gpt_answer:

Stormwild Capridor’s ability prevents only noncombat damage and grants +1/+1 counters for damage prevented that way, so it doesn’t prevent this combat damage and it doesn’t get +1/+1 counters for it [Stormwild Capridor; Stormwild Capridor ruling #1]. question: Alaia controls [Rielle, the Everwise] and casts [Kindle the Carnage]. While resolving Kindle the Carnage, Alaia chooses to discard a total of 3 cards, triggering Rielle, the Everwise. How many cards will Alaia draw when the trigger resolves?
gold:
Alaia will draw one card.

Each card that Alaia discards during the resolution of Kindle the Carnage constitutes its own discard event since they happen sequentially rather than all at the same time. Rielle, the Everwise will trigger after the first of these. Since only one card is discarded in that event, Alaia will draw one card from the trigger.
opus_answer:
Alaia draws 1 card.

Rielle, the Everwise reads "Whenever you discard one or more cards for the first time each turn, draw that many cards." Kindle the Carnage discards cards one at a time in separate iterations — you discard a card at random, see it, deal damage equal to its mana value to each creature, and only then decide whether to repeat (Kindle the Carnage ruling #3). So the three discards are three separate discard events, not one simultaneous discard of three cards.

The first of those discards is the first time Alaia discarded a card this turn, so Rielle, the Everwise triggers, and "that many" refers to the one card discarded in that event. The second and third discards are no longer "the first time each turn," so they don't trigger Rielle, the Everwise at all.

Timing: the trigger from the first discard happens during Kindle the Carnage's resolution, so it waits and goes on the stack after Kindle the Carnage finishes resolving (Rielle, the Everwise ruling #2, and generally a trigger whose event occurs during resolution goes on the stack after that spell finishes — see [603.8]/[704.4]). By then all three discards and all the damage have already happened, but that doesn't change the count: the trigger's "that many" was fixed by the single discard event that caused it, so Alaia draws exactly 1 card, one at a time ([121.2a]).

If instead all three cards had somehow been discarded simultaneously as a single event (which Kindle the Carnage does not do), Rielle, the Everwise would have triggered once for 3 cards.

This works identically at a two-player table and in multiplayer; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
gpt_answer: Alaia will draw 1 card when Rielle, the Everwise’s triggered ability resolves.

question: Ariel casts [Kathari Remnant] and reveals [Harrow] with the cascade trigger. Can they tap their lands for mana before sacrificing them?
gold: No. Harrow must be cast while the casade trigger is resolving, during which time no player gets priority. And since Harrow doesn't require a mana payment when it's being cast with cascade, Ariel doesn't get a chance to activate mana abilities.
opus_answer:
Short answer: No — not in this case. Because Kathari Remnant's cascade lets Ariel cast Harrow *without paying its mana cost*, Harrow's total cost contains no mana payment at all (just the additional cost "sacrifice a land"), and a player only gets a chance to activate mana abilities as part of casting when the cost includes a mana payment [118.2]. Ariel also doesn't receive priority while the cascade trigger is still resolving [608.2g], so there's no other window to tap lands and float mana before the sacrifice.

Details:

- Cascade on Kathari Remnant says you exile until you exile a nonland card with lesser mana value and "may cast that card without paying its mana cost"; exiling is mandatory, only the casting is optional [702.85a][Kathari Remnant ruling #0].
- Casting Harrow this way still follows the normal casting steps 601.2a–i, except no player gets priority afterward [608.2g]. Harrow's additional cost — sacrifice a land — is not waived by "without paying its mana cost"; it's part of the total cost determined at 601.2f and paid at 601.2h [601.2f][601.2h][Harrow ruling #1].
- Ariel chooses which land to sacrifice while making choices for the spell and then sacrifices it as the total cost is paid [601.2h][601.5]. Since {2}{G} isn't being paid, there is no mana component and therefore no mana-ability window inside the casting process [118.2].
- Contrast: if Ariel were casting Harrow normally for {2}{G} plus sacrificing a land, they would get a chance to activate mana abilities during payment [118.2], and they could tap a land for mana and then sacrifice that same tapped land, since the mana stays in the pool and the total cost is already locked in [601.2f][601.2h]. Triggered mana abilities from those taps resolve immediately and can help pay [605.4a].
- Timing note: I'm assuming Ariel wants to tap lands during the cascade-driven casting of Harrow. If instead they tapped lands for mana *earlier*, while casting Kathari Remnant or while they had priority before cascade resolved, that mana is already in their pool and those lands can still be sacrificed to Harrow's additional cost — but they can't create that window once cascade has begun resolving [608.2g].
- If Ariel can't sacrifice a land at all, the casting of Harrow is illegal and is reversed [601.2h][733.1]; the exiled cards that weren't cast go to the bottom of the library in a random order [702.85a].

Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
gpt_answer:
No — if you cast Harrow via Kathari Remnant’s cascade “without paying its mana cost,” you do not get to tap lands for mana before sacrificing them. You may only tap lands first if you instead choose to cast Harrow by paying its mana cost (i.e., you include a mana payment as part of the cost). 

Reasoning (assumptions: cascade’s cast-by-resolution timing): Kathari Remnant’s cascade lets you exile cards and then “may cast that card without paying its mana cost” (cascade) as that cascade ability resolves; when an effect lets you cast a spell during resolution you follow the normal casting steps in rules 601.2a–i (so you either cast Harrow and pay its mana cost and additional costs, or you cast Harrow without paying its mana cost and still pay any additional costs) [702.85a, 702.85b, 608.2g, 601.2a]. Harrow’s sacrifice of a land is an additional cost to cast Harrow (it is part of the cost) [Harrow ruling #1]. When casting a spell you determine the total cost and then pay costs; sacrifices required by the cost are chosen as you make choices for the spell and are sacrificed as you pay the total cost (you don’t sacrifice earlier) [601.2f, 601.2h, 702.48b]. A player gets an opportunity to activate mana abilities to produce mana when a cost includes a mana payment (so they may activate mana abilities to help pay a mana cost) [118.2]. Therefore: if you cast Harrow via Kathari Remnant’s cascade and choose to cast it without paying Harrow’s mana cost, there is no mana payment to make and so you do not get the explicit opportunity to activate mana abilities to produce mana before paying the (non-mana) sacrifice cost; the land is chosen during casting and is sacrificed when you pay the spell’s costs [601.2a, 601.2f, 601.2h, 702.48b, Harrow ruling #1]. If you instead choose to cast Harrow by paying its mana cost, that mana payment gives you the opportunity to activate mana abilities (you could tap lands for mana first), and then you would pay the sacrifice as part of paying the total cost [118.2, 601.2f, 601.2h].

question: Neil controls [Confounding Conundrum]. Averi hasn't played a land this turn and casts [Circuitous Route]. How many lands get returned to Averi's hand?
gold: Two. Since the lands enter at the same time and such will both trigger Confounding Conundrum since triggered abilities check to see if they trigger after the event happens.
opus_answer:
Two lands — Averi returns two lands they control to their owner's hand.

Why: Circuitous Route says "search your library for up to two basic land cards and/or Gate cards, put them onto the battlefield tapped." Assuming Averi finds and puts two lands onto the battlefield, they enter simultaneously. Note that this is putting lands onto the battlefield, not playing a land, so it doesn't use Averi's land drop for the turn (305.4, 701.18a) — but Confounding Conundrum doesn't care about playing lands, only about lands entering.

Confounding Conundrum's second ability triggers "whenever a land an opponent controls enters, if that player had another land enter the battlefield under their control this turn." Per [Confounding Conundrum ruling #1], if an opponent has had no lands enter and then two or more lands enter at the same time, the ability triggers for each of those lands. So with two lands from Circuitous Route, Confounding Conundrum triggers twice, and each trigger makes Averi return a land they control to its owner's hand — two lands total.

Per [Confounding Conundrum ruling #0], Averi chooses any lands they control, not necessarily the two that just entered from Circuitous Route. Note the triggered abilities from Confounding Conundrum use the stack, and Neil (as Confounding Conundrum's controller) controls the triggers, but Averi makes the choice of which lands to return.

If Averi only finds one land with Circuitous Route (or none), Confounding Conundrum wouldn't trigger at all with a satisfied condition, since no other land would have entered under Averi's control this turn.

Multiplayer note: Confounding Conundrum reads "a land an opponent controls," so it works the same whether the game has two players or more — it just applies to each of Neil's opponents, and any other opponent putting in multiple lands would be affected identically.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
gpt_answer:
If Circuitous Route finds and puts two lands onto the battlefield, Averi must return two lands to their hand (one for each triggered ability). If Circuitous Route puts only one land onto the battlefield, Averi returns no lands.

Reasoning and assumptions:
- Circuitous Route’s resolution instructs Averi to “put” up to two basic land cards and/or Gate cards onto the battlefield tapped, so those lands enter the battlefield as part of the sorcery’s resolution (Circuitous Route). [I assume Averi chose two lands; if they chose only one, see below.]
- A triggered ability triggers automatically when its trigger event occurs (a land entering the battlefield is such an event), and it can trigger multiple times if the event contains multiple occurrences (603.2c). Confounding Conundrum’s ability reads “Whenever a land an opponent controls enters, if that player had another land enter the battlefield under their control this turn, they return a land they control to its owner's hand.”
- The comprehensive ruling for Confounding Conundrum says that if an opponent has had no lands enter under their control and then two or more lands enter at the same time, Confounding Conundrum’s second ability triggers for each of those lands (Confounding Conundrum ruling #1). Therefore, when Circuitous Route puts two lands onto the battlefield simultaneously, Confounding Conundrum will produce two separate triggers.
- Each of those triggers instructs Averi to return a land they control to its owner’s hand; the Confounding Conundrum rulings state Averi may return any lands they control (not only the ones that just entered) for each trigger (Confounding Conundrum ruling #0). So two triggers = Averi returns two lands.
- If Circuitous Route puts only one land onto the battlefield, the condition “if that player had another land enter the battlefield under their control this turn” is false for that single entering land, so no triggers occur and no lands are returned.
- Note: these are lands being “put” onto the battlefield by an effect, not “played” as a land, which is a different action (305.4; 701.18a). This distinction doesn’t stop the lands from entering the battlefield and causing Confounding Conundrum’s triggers.

If you want the precise wording I relied on, see the cited rules and card rulings below.

question: Agustin uses [Gideon, Ally of Zendikar]'s [+1] ability to turn it into a creature in their precombat main phase and attaches [Helm of the Host] to it. What is the copy that's made by Helm of the Host?
gold: The copy of Gideon, Ally of Zendikar will be a non-legendary planeswalker with haste; it is not a creature.
opus_answer:
The token is a copy of the printed card Gideon, Ally of Zendikar — i.e., a nonlegendary planeswalker token named Gideon, Ally of Zendikar with loyalty 4 and its three loyalty abilities — and it is NOT a 5/5 creature. It does gain haste from Helm of the Host, but haste does nothing relevant since the token isn't a creature and can't attack.

Why: Helm of the Host's trigger creates "a token that's a copy of equipped creature, except the token isn't legendary." A copy uses only the copiable values, which are the values derived from the text printed on the object as modified by other copy effects, face-down status, and "as ... enters" abilities that set power and toughness; other effects, including type-changing effects, plus status and counters, are not copied [707.2a] [707.2] [613.2a] [613.2c]. Gideon, Ally of Zendikar's +1 ability is a type-changing (and power/toughness-setting) continuous effect, not a copiable value, so the token doesn't get "5/5 Human Soldier Ally creature with indestructible" or the damage prevention [Gideon, Ally of Zendikar ruling #1] [Helm of the Host ruling #5]. Helm of the Host's own "except the token isn't legendary" exception is a modification to the copying process, and that modified value becomes part of the token's copiable values [707.9b] [707.9c].

Practical results: the token enters as a planeswalker with 4 starting loyalty (loyalty counters on the original aren't copied), it isn't legendary so it doesn't die to the legend rule alongside the original, and Agustin may activate one loyalty ability of the token that turn — including its own +1 to make it a 5/5 creature, though it couldn't attack this turn under the summoning-sickness restriction on Gideon-style creatures [Gideon, Ally of Zendikar ruling #0]. Note also that Helm of the Host makes the token at the beginning of combat on Agustin's turn, so the +1 must have been used in the precombat main phase (as stated) for Gideon to be a creature to legally carry the Equipment.

If the equipped Gideon, Ally of Zendikar has left the battlefield before the Helm of the Host trigger resolves, no token is made [Helm of the Host ruling #1].

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
gpt_answer:
Direct answer: Helm of the Host will create a nonlegendary token that is a copy of Gideon, Ally of Zendikar as printed — i.e., a nonlegendary planeswalker named Gideon, Ally of Zendikar with its printed loyalty and printed abilities. The token is not a creature even though Gideon, Ally of Zendikar was made a creature that turn; Helm’s “except the token isn’t legendary” modification still applies, and the token gains haste per Helm of the Host.

Why: A “copy” is an object created to be a copy of another object (see rule [707.1]); copying uses the copiable values derived from the text printed on the original object (see rule [707.2]). Helm of the Host’s token-creation copies the printed characteristics of the equipped object (Helm of the Host’s text and rulings), and Helm of the Host’s ruling #5 explicitly states the token copies exactly what was printed on the original and nothing else. The temporary effect from activating Gideon, Ally of Zendikar’s +1 (that causes Gideon, Ally of Zendikar to “become” a 5/5 Human Soldier Ally creature until end of turn) is not part of what is copied in this situation: the official copying guidance and examples (see rule [707.2]) show that becoming a creature via an effect does not cause a copy to be created as a creature. In addition, Gideon, Ally of Zendikar’s ruling #1 confirms that the +1 makes Gideon, Ally of Zendikar a creature while he remains a planeswalker; that status on the battlefield is a result of effects, not printed copiable values. Because Helm of the Host also says the token “isn’t legendary,” the created token will be a nonlegendary planeswalker named Gideon, Ally of Zendikar with Gideon, Ally of Zendikar’s printed loyalty and printed abilities; it will not be a creature.

If you want the short practical outcome: you get a nonlegendary planeswalker token copy of Gideon, Ally of Zendikar (with haste from Helm of the Host), not a creature token.

Caveat about timing: this assumes Gideon, Ally of Zendikar’s +1 was activated in the precombat main and is still an effect that would make him a creature that turn when Helm’s trigger resolves at the beginning of combat. The conclusion (that the token is a copy of the printed card and not a creature) doesn’t change under different timing — copying uses the printed/copiable values, not battlefield-applied temporary creature status (see [707.2] example).

question: Ainsley controls a [Gaea's Cradle] enchanted by a [Market Festival] and no creatures. If Ainsley taps the Gaea's Cradle, how much mana is produced?
gold: No mana is produced. Gaea's Cradle's activated ability is not producing any mana, so Market Festival doesn't trigger.
opus_answer:
Ainsley produces no mana at all — zero from Gaea's Cradle and nothing from Market Festival.

Why: Gaea's Cradle's ability is "{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control." With no creatures, the amount is zero, so the ability adds no mana (compare the Viridian Joiner example in [107.1b], where a power-based mana ability adds no mana). It's still a mana ability even though it produces nothing [605.2], and it still resolves immediately without using the stack [405.6c].

Market Festival says "Whenever enchanted land is tapped for mana, its controller adds an additional two mana in any combination of colors." To "tap a permanent for mana" is to activate a mana ability with {T} in its cost, and such a trigger only triggers when that mana ability resolves **and produces mana** [106.12a, 106.12b]. Since Gaea's Cradle's ability resolved producing no mana, Market Festival's triggered ability never triggers, so no additional two mana are added. (Had it triggered, it would be a triggered mana ability that resolves immediately without going on the stack, per [605.4a].)

If Ainsley controlled even one creature, Gaea's Cradle would produce {G} for each creature, Market Festival would trigger, and Ainsley would add two more mana in any combination of colors.

This outcome is identical in two-player and multiplayer games; nothing here depends on opponents or the number of players.

gpt_answer:
No mana is produced—Ainsley gets 0 mana. Gaea's Cradle’s {T} ability would add {G} for each creature Ainsley controls, and with no creatures that ability produces no mana; Market Festival’s triggered ability doesn’t trigger because the land wasn’t effectively “tapped for mana” (no mana was produced). 

Explanation and definitions: To “tap [a permanent] for mana” means to activate a mana ability of that permanent that includes the {T} symbol in its activation cost ([106.12a]). Gaea's Cradle’s ability is such a mana ability: “{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control.” Because Ainsley controls zero creatures, Gaea's Cradle’s ability produces zero {G} (it is still a mana ability even if it produces no mana) ([605.2]; Gaea's Cradle). Market Festival’s text, “Whenever enchanted land is tapped for mana, its controller adds an additional two mana…,” is a triggered mana ability that triggers only when the land’s mana ability resolves and produces mana ([106.12a]; Market Festival). Because Gaea's Cradle produced no mana, Market Festival’s trigger does not occur, so no additional mana is added ([605.4a]; Market Festival). 

Therefore total mana produced = 0.

question: Alex casts [Fires of Undeath] from their graveyard for its flashback cost and Nelson exiles it with [Spell Queller]. If Spell Queller dies later in the turn, can Alex cast the Fires of Undeath? If so, what zone will it move to as it resolves?
gold: Alex can cast it. It was exiled by Spell Queller's ability- flashback doesn't affect that. It's a different object from when it was previously on the stack, so flashback's replacement effect doesn't apply to it anymore. It will be put into the graveyard when it resolves.
opus_answer:
Yes — Alex may cast Fires of Undeath, and this time it goes to Alex's graveyard as it resolves (not exile).

Details:

1) Casting it. Spell Queller's leaves-the-battlefield trigger says the exiled card's owner may cast that card without paying its mana cost. Alex must cast it right then, as part of that trigger's resolution — Alex can't hold it to cast later in the turn — and timing permissions based on card type are ignored (Fires of Undeath is an instant anyway) [Spell Queller ruling #1]. Alex casts it from the exile zone, putting it on the stack [112.1], [601.2b].

2) Why it isn't exiled again. Flashback means "you may cast this card from your graveyard by paying [cost] rather than its mana cost" and "if the flashback cost was paid, exile this card instead of putting it anywhere else any time it would leave the stack" [Fires of Undeath ruling #3]. That replacement applied to the earlier spell, and it's why exiling it with Spell Queller stuck [Fires of Undeath ruling #5]. But once the card changed zones it became a new object with no memory of its previous existence [400.7k], and the new spell Alex casts has no relation to the original — choices and effects affecting the original spell don't carry over [Spell Queller ruling #0]. Alex is casting it from exile for Spell Queller's alternative cost of nothing, not paying a flashback cost, so no flashback replacement is active. It resolves normally and is put into its owner's graveyard.

3) If Alex declines to cast it, or if it's countered or otherwise leaves the stack, it simply goes to Alex's graveyard for the same reason (no flashback cost was paid for this casting).

Timing note: this assumes Spell Queller's enters-the-battlefield ability already resolved and actually exiled Fires of Undeath before Spell Queller died. If Spell Queller had left the battlefield before that ability resolved, the leaves-the-battlefield trigger would resolve first and do nothing, and then Fires of Undeath would be exiled forever with no chance to cast it [Spell Queller ruling #4].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players — the card's owner (Alex) is the one who gets the option, regardless of table size.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
gpt_answer:
Yes. When Spell Queller leaves the battlefield later in the turn, Alex may cast Fires of Undeath from exile as part of Spell Queller’s leaves-the-battlefield ability; that casting is a new casting that is not using Fires of Undeath’s flashback, and when that new casting resolves the Fires of Undeath card will go to its owner’s graveyard. 

Reasoning (assumptions and step-by-step):
- Flashback: “Flashback [cost]” on Fires of Undeath means “You may cast this card from your graveyard by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost,” and “If the flashback cost was paid, exile this card instead of putting it anywhere else any time it would leave the stack” (Fires of Undeath ruling #3). When Alex originally cast Fires of Undeath from the graveyard by paying its flashback cost, that casting caused the card to be exiled afterward per Fires of Undeath ruling #5. 
- Spell Queller’s interactions: Spell Queller’s leaves-the-battlefield triggered ability lets the owner of a card exiled by Spell Queller cast that exiled card without paying its mana cost as the ability resolves, and if the owner does cast it they do so as part of resolution of Spell Queller’s ability (Spell Queller ruling #1). The new casting is a separate spell with no relation to the original spell that was cast (Spell Queller ruling #0). 
- Casting from exile under Spell Queller’s ability: A card in exile that is the object allowed to be cast by Spell Queller’s ability can be cast from exile (112.1; 601.2b; 601.2f); the exceptions to the “new object” rule allow effects that grant the ability to cast a nonland card to apply to the new object after it moves to the stack (400.7h). Because Spell Queller’s ability lets Alex cast the exiled Fires of Undeath without paying its mana cost, Alex is not paying Fires of Undeath’s flashback cost for that casting, so the flashback-specific exile instruction (which applies only “If the flashback cost was paid”) does not apply to this new casting (Fires of Undeath ruling #3). 
- Resulting zone as it resolves: Because the casting caused by Spell Queller’s leaves-the-battlefield ability is a new casting that is not a flashback cast, the flashback replacement/exile requirement doesn’t apply to this casting; therefore, when that new spell resolves it will follow the normal outcome for a resolved spell (i.e., the Fires of Undeath card will be put into its owner’s graveyard rather than being exiled by the flashback rule). (See Spell Queller ruling #1 and Spell Queller ruling #0 for that this is a new, separate casting; see Fires of Undeath ruling #3 to note the flashback exile happens only when the flashback cost was paid.)

If instead Spell Queller had died and its leaves-the-battlefield ability tried to let Alex cast the card at a time when Alex wasn’t allowed to cast spells, Alex couldn’t begin that casting (601.3f). Also note—per Spell Queller ruling #1—Alex must cast the exiled Fires of Undeath as part of resolution of Spell Queller’s leaves-the-battlefield ability; Alex can’t wait to cast it later in the turn.

question: If Atticus uses [Halvar, God of Battle]'s ability to attach [Helm of the Host] to Halvar, God of Battle, will they get a token copy of it?
gold: It depends on the order in which Atticus puts the triggers onto the stack. If they have the Helm of the Host trigger resolve second, they will get a copy. Helm of the Host triggers at the beginning of combat regardless of whether it's attached to anything, and it makes a copy of whatever it's equipping on resolution.
opus_answer:
Yes — provided the Helm of the Host trigger resolves after Halvar, God of Battle's attach ability, Atticus gets a non-legendary token copy of Halvar, God of Battle with haste.

How the timing works: both Halvar, God of Battle's "At the beginning of each combat" ability and Helm of the Host's "At the beginning of combat on your turn" ability trigger at the same time, and both are controlled by Atticus, so Atticus chooses the order they go on the stack. Since the last ability put on the stack resolves first, Atticus should put Helm of the Host's trigger on the stack first so that Halvar, God of Battle's attach ability resolves first and moves Helm of the Host onto Halvar, God of Battle. Then, when Helm of the Host's trigger resolves, the "equipped creature" (rule 301.5f — the creature the Equipment is attached to) is Halvar, God of Battle, and the token copy is created.

If instead Helm of the Host's trigger resolves first, it copies whatever creature Helm of the Host was attached to at that moment (or no token at all if it was unattached — see Helm of the Host ruling #1), and the re-attachment to Halvar, God of Battle would only matter for a later combat.

Details on the token: it is a copy of Halvar, God of Battle except it isn't legendary, so the "legend rule" doesn't force Atticus to sacrifice one (Helm of the Host ruling #3). Being a modal double-faced card, the copy is of the face that was on the battlefield — the Halvar, God of Battle creature face. The token does not copy the Equipment or Auras attached to Halvar, God of Battle, counters on it, or non-copy effects (Helm of the Host ruling #5), so Helm of the Host stays attached to the original Halvar, God of Battle.

Also note Halvar, God of Battle's attach ability requires the Equipment to be attached to a creature you control and needs both an Equipment target and a creature target (Halvar, God of Battle // Sword of the Realms rulings #13 and #7); if Helm of the Host is currently unattached, it isn't a legal target and Atticus would need to use Equip {5} instead.

Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since both triggers are Atticus's own and he orders them himself.

gpt_answer:
Yes — you can get a token copy of Halvar, God of Battle if you use Halvar, God of Battle’s triggered ability to attach Helm of the Host to Halvar, God of Battle before Helm of the Host’s triggered ability resolves. The key point is that “equipped creature” means whatever creature Helm of the Host is attached to at the time Helm of the Host’s triggered ability resolves, so if Helm of the Host is attached to Halvar, God of Battle when that ability resolves, the token will be a copy of Halvar, God of Battle (the token won’t be legendary).

Reasoning and assumptions:
- “Equipped creature” is the creature an Equipment is attached to (definition: an Equipment can be attached only to a creature and an ability that refers to the “equipped creature” refers to whatever creature that permanent is attached to) [301.5f].
- Halvar, God of Battle’s beginning-of-combat triggered ability can target an Aura or Equipment that is attached to a creature you control and attach it to a target creature you control when it resolves [Halvar, God of Battle // Sword of the Realms ruling #13]. Equipment can be attached to creatures by spells or other abilities [301.5b].
- Helm of the Host’s triggered ability creates a token that is a copy of the equipped creature when that triggered ability resolves; if there is no equipped creature when the ability resolves, no token is created, and the token isn’t legendary in any case [Helm of the Host ruling #1; Helm of the Host ruling #5].

Therefore, if you arrange things so Halvar, God of Battle’s ability resolves first and attaches Helm of the Host to Halvar, God of Battle, then when Helm of the Host’s triggered ability resolves it will create a token copy of Halvar, God of Battle (not legendary). If instead Helm of the Host’s triggered ability resolves before Halvar, God of Battle’s ability moves Helm of the Host, the token will be a copy of whatever creature Helm of the Host was attached to when its ability resolved.

If any target of Halvar, God of Battle’s triggered ability is illegal as that ability resolves, Halvar’s ability won’t do anything (or won’t resolve if both targets are illegal) [Halvar, God of Battle // Sword of the Realms ruling #7].

question: Ashley casts [Aminatou's Augury] exiling an artifact and an instant. Afterwards Ashley casts another Aminatou's Augury, which exiles an instant. Can they cast both instants?
gold: Yes. Each Aminatou's Augury creates a separate effect that applies to cards it exiled. Casting an instant off the first Aminatou's Augury doesn't preclude Ashley from casting an instant off the second one.
opus_answer:
Yes — Ashley can cast both instants, as long as they do it during that same turn.

Why: each resolution of Aminatou's Augury creates its own separate permission that applies only to the cards that that particular Aminatou's Augury exiled. The ability that exiles the cards and the ability that lets you cast "a spell of that type from among the exiled cards" are linked abilities, so the second refers only to the cards exiled by that same instance of the ability, not to cards exiled by any other Aminatou's Augury [607.1, 607.2a, 406.6].

So:
- The first Aminatou's Augury lets Ashley cast, without paying its mana cost, one artifact spell and one instant spell from among its own eight exiled cards (one spell per nonland card type).
- The second Aminatou's Augury separately lets Ashley cast one instant spell from among its own exiled cards.

That's two different instants, each cast under a different permission — no conflict. Note that the first Aminatou's Augury's permission lasts only "until end of turn," and since the second Aminatou's Augury is a sorcery cast in the same main phase, both windows overlap for the rest of that turn. If the second Aminatou's Augury were cast on a later turn, the first instant's permission would already have expired.

Timing: normal timing rules still apply to each spell cast this way [Aminatou's Augury ruling #3], but instants can be cast any time Ashley has priority [304.1, 304.5], so both are castable during Ashley's turn. Also, each exiled card can only be cast once, since casting it moves it out of exile [Aminatou's Augury ruling #0, 601.2a].

This analysis is the same at a two-player or a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

gpt_answer:
Yes. Each Aminatou's Augury creates its own permission that applies only to the cards it exiled, so you may cast the instant exiled by the first Aminatou's Augury and you may also cast the instant exiled by the second Aminatou's Augury (subject to normal timing and priority).

Reasoning and definition of key terms
- “Linked abilities”: When an object’s text both exiles cards and then refers to “the exiled cards,” those parts are linked; the part that refers to the exiled cards refers only to the cards exiled by that same effect ([607.1], [607.2a]). Aminatou's Augury exiles cards and then grants permission to cast spells “from among the exiled cards,” so each Aminatou's Augury’s permission refers only to the specific cards that that copy of Aminatou's Augury exiled. 
- What happens when you cast an exiled card: Casting an exiled card causes it to leave the exile zone, and you can’t cast that same exiled card multiple times ([Aminatou's Augury ruling #0]).

Putting that together: the first Aminatou's Augury’s “until end of turn… you may cast a spell of that type from among the exiled cards without paying its mana cost” applies only to the cards exiled by that first Aminatou's Augury ([607.1], [607.2a]). The second Aminatou's Augury independently creates the analogous permission for the cards it exiled. Therefore you have permission to cast the instant exiled by the first Aminatou's Augury and also permission to cast the instant exiled by the second Aminatou's Augury. You must follow normal timing restrictions for each spell ([Aminatou's Augury ruling #3]) and you must be legally allowed to begin casting each spell when you attempt to do so ([601.3f]); when you cast one of those exiled spells it is moved to the stack as a spell and its total cost is determined (the Aminatou's Augury permission makes you cast it without paying its mana cost) as part of the normal casting process ([601.2a], [601.2f]).

Timing assumption: This answer assumes you mean the two Aminatou's Augury resolutions happened earlier in the turn and you now have priority to cast instants; if you cast one of the instants while you don’t have priority or when its timing is illegal, then it cannot be cast until a legal time ([Aminatou's Augury ruling #3], [601.3f]).

question: Avery activates [Merieke Ri Berit]'s ability, targeting Nataly's [Silverback Ape]. Before that ability resolves, Avery untaps Merieke Ri Berit with [Thousand-Year Elixir] and then taps it again targeting [Goblin Piker]. What happens to Silverback Ape and Goblin Piker?

Avery will gain control of Silverback Ape and Goblin Piker. Neither of them will be destroyed.

Merieke Ri Berit's ability creates a delayed trigger that triggers when Merieke Ri Berit becomes untapped. When Merieke Ri Berit became untapped its ability hadn't resolved yet, so there was no delayed trigger to destroy the Silverback Ape.
opus_answer:
Both Silverback Ape and Goblin Piker end up under Avery's control, and neither is destroyed by the untap that happened in between.

Why: Merieke Ri Berit's "destroy that creature" clause is a delayed triggered ability that only comes into existence when the {T} ability actually resolves and control is gained (603.7d). At the moment Avery untapped Merieke Ri Berit with Thousand-Year Elixir, the first activation (targeting Silverback Ape) was still on the stack, so no delayed trigger existed yet and nothing was destroyed.

Order of resolution: the second activation (targeting Goblin Piker) was activated in response to the first, so it resolves first (117.7). Then the first activation resolves: it still has a legal target, so Avery gains control of Silverback Ape and a second delayed trigger, keyed to Silverback Ape, is created (608.2b, 608.2c).

Going forward, Merieke Ri Berit is tapped and won't untap during Avery's untap step. If Merieke Ri Berit later leaves the battlefield or becomes untapped, both delayed triggers trigger and both Silverback Ape and Goblin Piker are destroyed and can't be regenerated — and Avery doesn't lose control of them before they're destroyed (Merieke Ri Berit ruling #0). Timing assumption: I'm assuming the untap and the second activation both happened while the first ability was still on the stack, as stated. If instead the first ability had already resolved before the untap, the delayed trigger for Silverback Ape would have existed and Silverback Ape would have been destroyed (uneregeneratably) when Merieke Ri Berit untapped, while Avery kept control of it until then.

6) Next the triggered “When Merieke Ri Berit … becomes untapped, destroy that creature” resolves. [Merieke Ri Berit]

question: Atlas controls [Master Biomancer], [Pir, Imaginative Rascal], and [Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider]. They cast [Corpsejack Menace]. How many +1/+1 counters does it enter the battlefield with?
gold: Either 5 or 6, depending on the order of the choices that Atlas makes. Master Biomancer's effect needs to be applied first since none of the other effects apply to Corpsejack Menace entering without counters. Corpsejack Menace has no effect on itself because it needs to be on the battlefield before a creature enters in order to apply to it. So the only choice Atlas has is whether to apply Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider's effect first and end up with 5 counters or to apply Pir, Imaginative Rascal's effect first and end up with 6 counters.
opus_answer:
Corpsejack Menace enters with either 6 or 5 +1/+1 counters, at Atlas's choice — 6 if Atlas applies Pir, Imaginative Rascal first, 5 if Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider is applied first.

How it works:

1. Base amount: Master Biomancer says each other creature Atlas controls enters with additional +1/+1 counters equal to Master Biomancer's power, measured as that creature enters [Master Biomancer ruling #0]. With Master Biomancer at 2/4, that's 2 counters. This is a replacement effect modifying how Corpsejack Menace enters [614.1c], [614.12].
2. Corpsejack Menace's own doubling ability does NOT apply to itself. A replacement effect from the entering permanent itself only applies if it affects only that permanent, not a general subset of permanents that happens to include it [614.12b]; Corpsejack Menace's ability refers to "a creature you control" generally, which is the same reason Orb of Dreams doesn't tap itself in the [614.12] example.
3. Pir, Imaginative Rascal (+1 of each kind) and Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider (double) both modify entering counters [Pir, Imaginative Rascal ruling #5], [Corpsejack Menace ruling #0]. Two applicable replacement effects means the affected object's controller, Atlas, picks the order, applying one at a time and then re-checking [616.1], [616.1f], [Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider ruling #0]. Each effect applies only once [614.5].
   - Pir, Imaginative Rascal then Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider: 2 → 3 → 6.
   - Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider then Pir, Imaginative Rascal: 2 → 4 → 5.

So Atlas will normally choose 6.

Assumption: Master Biomancer's power is its printed 2 with no other buffs; if its power is different, substitute that number as the starting amount before Pir, Imaginative Rascal and Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider apply.

Player count doesn't matter here — all the relevant effects are Atlas's own, and Atlas alone makes the ordering choice. APNAP order [101.4] would only matter if other players had simultaneous choices to make.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
gpt_answer:
It enters the battlefield with 12 +1/+1 counters. 

Why: A replacement effect from Master Biomancer makes Corpsejack Menace enter with additional +1/+1 counters equal to Master Biomancer's power; use Master Biomancer's power as the entering creature is entering, which is 2, so the base number of counters to be put is 2 (Master Biomancer ruling #0; see rule 614.12 about effects that modify how a permanent enters). Multiple replacement effects then modify how many counters are put. Pir, Imaginative Rascal changes “would put N counters” into “put N+1 counters” (Pir, Imaginative Rascal ruling #5). Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider and Corpsejack Menace each replace “would put N counters” with “put twice that many” (Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider ruling #0; Corpsejack Menace ruling #0). When two or more effects attempt to modify how many counters would be put on a permanent you control, that permanent’s controller chooses the order to apply those effects (616.1; Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider ruling #0). Atlas (the controller) can therefore choose to apply Pir, Imaginative Rascal’s “+1” first: 2 -> 3, then apply the two doubling effects (Corpsejack Menace and Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider) in either order, doubling twice: 3 -> 6 -> 12. The replacement-application process is the repeated choose-and-apply procedure described in rules 616.1/616.1f and the modifications to how the creature enters are replacement effects as described in rule 614.1c and 614.12. 

(Note: different application orders yield different totals — e.g., applying the two doublings before Pir, Imaginative Rascal would give 9 — but Atlas chooses the order, so Atlas will get 12.)

question: Aleah attacks with a [Cloak and Dagger, Entwined] enchanted with [Lifelink]. How much life will Aleah gain?
gold: Aleah will gain 2 life. Additional occurrences of lifelink are redundant.
opus_answer:
Aleah gains 2 life (a single life-gain event of 2), assuming Cloak and Dagger, Entwined is unblocked or its 2 combat damage is dealt in full to a blocker.

Note that it's the controller of the enchanted creature who gains the life, not the controller of the Lifelink Aura if those are different players [Lifelink ruling #0]; since Aleah controls Cloak and Dagger, Entwined, Aleah gains the life.

Because this is one source dealing damage once, it's one life-gain event of 2, not two events of 2 — separate life-gain events only arise from multiple lifelink sources dealing damage simultaneously [702.15e]. That matters for "whenever you gain life" triggers, which would trigger once here [119.9].

If Cloak and Dagger, Entwined is blocked, its deathtouch means 1 damage is lethal for assignment purposes, but it still assigns all 2 of its combat damage to the blocker(s) it's fighting [510.1c], so Aleah still gains 2 life. If some of the damage is prevented or the creature's power is changed before damage, the life gained equals the damage actually dealt [120.4d]. This answer doesn't depend on player count; in a multiplayer game the same 2 life is gained regardless of which opponent is being attacked.

question: In Aspen's draw step, they tap [Vault of Catlacan] for 8 blue mana and cast [Time Stop]. Aspen discards a [Guile] to hand size. Can they use the two remaining {U} to cast an instant?

No — those two {U} are gone by the time anyone could cast anything.

Why: Time Stop reads "End the turn," which uses the end-the-turn process. That process ends the current phase or step (Aspen's draw step) immediately and skips straight to the cleanup step, and no player gets priority during the process, so nothing can be cast while it's happening [724.1][724.1d][724.1f]. As the draw step ends, "until end of step" effects expire and any unspent mana in each player's mana pool empties as a turn-based action [500.5]. There is still a priority window afterward, but not with that mana. Aspen discarding Guile to hand size is part of the end-the-turn process, and Guile's own text — "When Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner's library" — triggers. Because a triggered ability triggered during the process, that ability goes on the stack during the cleanup step, then the active player gets priority and players may cast spells and activate abilities [724.1f][514.3][514.3a]. At that point Aspen could cast an instant, but only by producing mana then — and Vault of Catlacan is already tapped from making the 8 blue, so it can't be tapped again for {U}. (Had nothing triggered, no player would have gotten priority in that cleanup step at all [724.1f].)

Timing note: I'm assuming the 8 blue was floating in the draw step when Time Stop resolved. If instead Aspen somehow had a mana source untapped or produced mana during the cleanup-step priority window, they could cast an instant then — but never with the pre-Time Stop mana.

This works the same at a two-player table and in multiplayer; the end-the-turn process and the mana-emptying rule don't depend on the number of players.

Therefore, Amira can’t dredge the token copy of Greater Mossdog after Dregs of Sorrow destroys it, because there is no Greater Mossdog card in a graveyard to have its Dredge ability function.

question: Aminah has no cards in their library and activate [Words of Wind] in their upkeep. Do they lose the game?

opus_answer:

An effect that replaces a card draw is applied even if no cards could be drawn because the affected player's library is empty [121.6a] [614.11]. Because the draw is replaced, Aminah never actually attempts to draw from the empty library, so the state-based action that makes a player lose for drawing from an empty library never triggers [704.5b] [121.4] [104.3c].

Assuming Aminah activates it during their own upkeep step, the replacement is set up before the draw step's turn-based action, in which the active player draws a card [504.1]. That draw is the "next time you would draw a card," so it is replaced by each player returning a permanent they control to its owner's hand, and Aminah survives the draw step. Each activation replaces only one draw, so a second draw that turn (or the next turn's draw step) with an empty library would still cause Aminah to lose the game the next time a player would receive priority unless another replacement is set up [704.5b] [121.4].

In a multiplayer game the answer is the same for Aminah; note that Words of Wind's effect makes each player, not just Aminah, return a permanent they control to its owner's hand, so more permanents bounce at a larger table.
