- Draw means “to put the top card of a player’s library into their hand as a turn-based action or as the result of an effect that uses the word ‘draw.’” [Draw].
- Words of Wind’s text reads: “{1}: The next time you would draw a card this turn, each player returns a permanent they control to its owner’s hand instead.” Because Words of Wind replaces that draw with returning permanents, the draw is replaced and does not happen as a draw (Words of Wind).

question: Alyson casts [Harm's Way], choosing [Caldera Lake] as the source of damage and Nixon as the target. After it resolves, Alyson taps Caldera Lake for {R}. Is Nixon dealt 1 damage?

opus_answer:
Yes. Tapping Caldera Lake for {R} makes Caldera Lake deal 1 damage to Alyson, and Harm's Way redirects that damage to Nixon instead, so Nixon is dealt 1 damage.

Details:

A permanent such as Caldera Lake is a legal choice for a source of damage, and a source doesn't need to be able to deal damage to be chosen [609.7a] [120.7].

- This is a redirection effect: a replacement effect that causes damage that would be dealt to one recipient to be dealt to another instead [614.9] [Redirection Effect]. Since only 1 damage is dealt, Harm's Way redirects that 1 and still has a "shield" left for 1 more damage from Caldera Lake later this turn [Harm's Way ruling #3].
- Caveat: if Nixon is no longer in the game (or, for a permanent target, is no longer a legal damage recipient) at the moment Caldera Lake would deal the damage, the damage isn't redirected and is dealt to Alyson instead [Harm's Way ruling #2] [614.9].
- Timing note: I'm assuming the tap for {R} happens after Harm's Way has resolved, as stated. If Caldera Lake had already dealt damage to Alyson before Harm's Way resolved, Harm's Way would do nothing about that already-dealt damage [Harm's Way ruling #1].
- Player count doesn't matter here: this works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Harm's Way just needs "any target."

This land deals 1 damage to you.” means tapping Caldera Lake for {R} causes Caldera Lake to deal 1 damage to Alyson (the controller) (Caldera Lake). question: Alvaro uses [Gideon, Martial Paragon]'s ability to turn it into a creature. They then put a +1/+1 counter on it with [Experiment Kraj] and activate Experiment Kraj's [+2] ability, putting two loyalty counters on it. After passing the turn, what will happen if they block an attacking creature with Experiment Kraj?

opus_answer:
Blocking with Experiment Kraj is completely ordinary: Experiment Kraj blocks as a 5/7 (its printed 4/6 plus the one +1/+1 counter), deals and receives combat damage normally, and the two loyalty counters sitting on it do nothing at all.

Why:

- Loyalty counters only matter on a planeswalker. The number of loyalty counters on a planeswalker indicates its loyalty [122.1e], and the state-based action that puts a permanent into the graveyard at 0 loyalty applies only to planeswalkers [704.5i, 306.9, 704.1]. Experiment Kraj is a creature, not a planeswalker, so its loyalty counters are inert markers.
- Combat damage dealt to Experiment Kraj does not remove those loyalty counters. Removing loyalty counters is a result of damage dealt to a planeswalker [306.8, 120.3c]. Damage to Experiment Kraj is simply marked on it, and Experiment Kraj is destroyed as a state-based action only if marked damage equals or exceeds its toughness of 7 [120.6].
- Gideon, Martial Paragon's creature-making ability lasts "until end of turn," so by the opponent's turn Gideon, Martial Paragon is a planeswalker again and not a creature. Experiment Kraj's ability only grants it the activated abilities of other creatures with a +1/+1 counter, so Experiment Kraj no longer has Gideon, Martial Paragon's loyalty abilities during that combat. (Gideon, Martial Paragon's damage-prevention from that same ability was also only for that turn — see [Gideon, Martial Paragon ruling #5] for how damage interacts with him while he is both a creature and a planeswalker.)

Timing assumption: I'm reading the block as happening on a later turn, after Gideon, Martial Paragon's "until end of turn" effect has expired. If instead Experiment Kraj somehow blocked during the same turn Gideon, Martial Paragon was animated, Experiment Kraj would still be a 5/7 creature whose loyalty counters do nothing — the only difference is that Experiment Kraj would still be copying Gideon, Martial Paragon's activated abilities.

Player count: nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer game; the block and damage work the same regardless of how many opponents are at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
gpt_answer:
Direct answer: Nothing special happens to Gideon, Martial Paragon when Experiment Kraj blocks. Experiment Kraj simply blocks the attacking creature as a normal blocking creature; Gideon, Martial Paragon is no longer a creature after the turn in which you used his 0 ability ended, so he isn’t involved in that combat and won’t gain or lose loyalty because of that block.

Reasoning and details:
- Gideon, Martial Paragon’s 0 ability made Gideon, Martial Paragon a creature “until end of turn” (he was both a creature and a planeswalker while that effect lasted) [Gideon, Martial Paragon]. After that turn ended, that effect ended and Gideon, Martial Paragon stopped being a creature (he remained a planeswalker) [Gideon, Martial Paragon ruling #0].
- Experiment Kraj’s text grants Experiment Kraj the activated abilities of each other creature that currently has a +1/+1 counter on it [Experiment Kraj]. That granted set of abilities depends on those other permanents actually being creatures with a +1/+1 counter at the time the continuous effect applies; once Gideon, Martial Paragon stops being a creature, Experiment Kraj no longer has any activated abilities it only had because Gideon, Martial Paragon was a creature with a +1/+1 counter [Experiment Kraj ruling #0]. (That’s why you could earlier use Experiment Kraj to interact with Gideon, Martial Paragon while Gideon, Martial Paragon was a creature with a +1/+1 counter, but not later once Gideon, Martial Paragon isn’t a creature.)
- When Experiment Kraj blocks an attacking creature, combat damage will be assigned and dealt between that attacker and Experiment Kraj in the normal way. Because Gideon, Martial Paragon is not being attacked or dealt combat damage in that situation, no loyalty counters are removed from Gideon, Martial Paragon. (If a planeswalker is dealt damage, that many loyalty counters are removed from it [120.3c; 306.8], and if a planeswalker ever has 0 loyalty it’s put into its owner’s graveyard [704.5i; 306.9].) Gideon, Martial Paragon being a planeswalker only at that later time means the combat between the attacker and Experiment Kraj does not interact with Gideon, Martial Paragon.

If you want a different timing assumed: this answer assumes the block happens on a later turn after Gideon, Martial Paragon’s “until end of turn” effect has expired. If the block instead happened during the same turn while Gideon, Martial Paragon was still a creature (i.e., before end of that turn), combat damage to Gideon, Martial Paragon could both be marked on him as a creature and cause loyalty loss as a planeswalker per the card ruling [Gideon, Martial Paragon ruling #5].

question: Alex controls [Mycosynth Lattice], an [Animate Dead] attached to a [Skyshroud Troopers] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. How it gets there:

Mizzium Transreliquat used its {1}{U}{R} ability ("becomes a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability"), so its copiable values are Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus the {1}{U}{R} ability. A copy of Mizzium Transreliquat copies the result of copy effects already applying to it (Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #3), so Copy Artifact entered with those values, plus Copy Artifact's own modification making it an enchantment in addition to its other types, which becomes part of the copy's copiable values [707.9b]. Note that Mycosynth Lattice is what makes Animate Dead a legal copy target at all — Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1). Strictly, Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' enter-as-a-copy ability requires a *creature* you control, and Animate Dead is an artifact but not a creature, so the only way to end up copying Animate Dead while keeping the {1}{U}{R} ability is by activating that {1}{U}{R} ability. I'm assuming, as your question states, that the Copy Artifact permanent legitimately became a copy of Animate Dead and that Animate Dead's enters trigger resolved, losing "enchant creature card in a graveyard," gaining "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," returning Foot Soldiers and attaching to it. (If instead the copy of Animate Dead came about after it was already on the battlefield, the "When this Aura enters" trigger would never have triggered and Foot Soldiers would never have been returned.)
2. Because the {1}{U}{R} ability says "except it has this ability," the permanent still has that ability after becoming Animate Dead (Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #0), so it can be activated targeting Skyshroud Troopers — legal, since Mycosynth Lattice makes Skyshroud Troopers an artifact.
3. When that ability resolves, the permanent's copiable values are wholly overwritten by Skyshroud Troopers' (plus the {1}{U}{R} ability). It is no longer an enchantment, no longer an Aura, and no longer has Animate Dead's abilities or the "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura" text. Since it isn't an Aura, the state-based action that puts an Aura attached to an illegal object into its owner's graveyard doesn't apply to it [704.5m], [704.1], and the "an Aura that's also a creature can't enchant anything" rule likewise no longer applies to it as an Aura [303.4d]. It is simply a 3/3 Skyshroud Troopers copy with "{T}: Add {G}" and the {1}{U}{R} ability. Note that under Mycosynth Lattice it is colorless (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2).
4. Foot Soldiers was put onto the battlefield by the Animate Dead copy, but nothing now makes its controller sacrifice it, so it stays.

Caveat: Animate Dead's ruling that it goes to the graveyard as a state-based action applies only when it can't legally attach on entering (Animate Dead ruling #0) — that's not the case here. Nothing in this interaction depends on the number of players; it plays out the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

gpt_answer:

- Copy Artifact entered the battlefield as a copy of Animate Dead and, per Animate Dead’s rules text and rule 608.3c, its enters-the-battlefield effect returned Foot Soldiers from the graveyard to the battlefield and attached Copy Artifact to Foot Soldiers. [608.3c] [Copy Artifact ruling #2]

question: Ariel exiles [Rain-Slicked Copse] with [Brazen Cannonade]. Can they cycle Rain-Slicked Copse?

Cycling is an activated ability that functions only while the card with cycling is in a player's hand; "Cycling {2}" means "{2}, Discard this card: Draw a card" (rule 702.29a). Rain-Slicked Copse is in the exile zone, not Ariel's hand, so its cycling ability simply can't be activated there. The ability still exists on the card in exile for purposes of effects that care about a card having an activated ability (rule 702.29b), but that doesn't let Ariel use it.

Brazen Cannonade's Raid ability says "Until end of combat on your next turn, you may play that card." Playing a card means casting it as a spell or playing it as a land — for Rain-Slicked Copse, which is a Land — Forest Island, that means playing it as a land (using Ariel's land drop, entering tapped per its own text). It does not grant permission to activate cycling from exile. Unlike plot, which has a specific rule allowing its ability to function in another zone (rule 702.170f), no such permission exists here for cycling.

So Ariel's options are: play Rain-Slicked Copse as a land during the allowed window, or let it stay in exile. If Rain-Slicked Copse somehow returns to Ariel's hand later, cycling becomes available again.

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Addison has cast a sideboard card from [Glittering Wish], which is now in their graveyard. Addison then restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?

opus_answer:
The card Addison brought in with Glittering Wish stays in the game and becomes part of Addison's deck for the new game. Because all Magic cards involved in the game when it ended are involved in the new game — even cards that weren't originally part of it — the wished-for card is shuffled into Addison's library as the new game begins, and Addison still owns it [727.2]. Rule 727.2 gives exactly this example with Living Wish: a creature card brought in from outside the game is part of that player's library when the new game begins. Glittering Wish itself (in the graveyard, or in exile if it had exiled itself) and Karn Liberated likewise go back into Addison's deck and are shuffled in [727.2], [Karn Liberated ruling #9].

How the restart plays out: the old game immediately ends with no winner, loser, or draw, and all players still in the game start a new game using the normal starting procedure, except that Addison — who controlled the Karn Liberated ability — is the starting player [727.1], [727.1a], [104.6], [Karn Liberated ruling #12], [Karn Liberated ruling #9]. Everyone shuffles, resets to the format's starting life total, draws seven, and may mulligan [Karn Liberated ruling #9].

The one exception is Karn Liberated's own text, which overrides the general "all cards are involved" rule: non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated's +4 or −3 abilities remain in exile through the restart and are then put onto the battlefield under Addison's control [727.5], [Karn Liberated ruling #6]. Those cards are not in anyone's deck as the new game begins [727.5]. This happens after the pregame procedure but just before the first turn's untap step; no player has priority then, and anything that triggers goes on the stack at the beginning of the first upkeep step [727.4], [Karn Liberated ruling #4]. So if the card Addison wished for had been exiled by Karn Liberated and is a non-Aura permanent card, it would enter the battlefield under Addison's control instead of going into the library.

With more than two players the same thing happens for every player still in the game, and any player who had already left the game before the restart is not part of the new game [727.7], [Karn Liberated ruling #11]. Restarting also ignores the limited range of influence option — all players in the game are involved [801.17].

gpt_answer:

[Glittering Wish ruling #0] Rule 727.2 says that all Magic cards involved in the game that was restarted — including cards that were brought into the game from outside it — are involved in the new game and gives the Living Wish example showing such a card becomes part of that player’s library when the new game begins. I assume the timing is that Karn Liberated’s restart ability resolves and the game restarts in the usual way described in the cited rules; the answer would be the same if the card were on the battlefield, in hand, graveyard, or exile at the moment the game ended, because rule 727.2 treats all those cards as involved in the restarted game. Reasoning and relevant definitions/steps:
- A triggered ability is written “[When/Whenever/At] [trigger condition or event], [effect].” and triggers when its trigger event occurs (definition: triggered ability) [603.1].
- Stasis Snare’s triggered ability triggers when Stasis Snare enters the battlefield; that trigger is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [603.3d].
- Targets for a triggered ability are chosen as the ability is put on the stack [115.1d]. By that time the event that caused the trigger (both permanents entering) has completed, so Fusion Elemental is on the battlefield and can be targeted by Stasis Snare’s triggered ability.
- Zone-change triggers look for objects in the zone they moved to when the triggered ability resolves; if the object isn’t in that zone when the ability resolves the part that affects that object will do nothing [603.6b, 603.6d]. - This is different from a replacement effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield and must choose other objects as they enter; such replacement effects can’t choose objects that are entering at the same time (example and rule) [614.13a]. Assumption: I’m assuming the normal timing where Show and Tell’s effect finishes putting both chosen permanents onto the battlefield simultaneously; under that timing the above applies. If permanents did not end up on the battlefield (for example, one was prevented from entering), then that permanent wouldn’t be a legal target when the triggered ability is put on the stack [603.6b, 603.6d].

question: Audrey casts [Nature's Lore] and puts [Dryad Arbor] onto the battlefield. Nico controls [Uphill Battle]. Does the Dryad Arbor enter the battlefield tapped?

Multiplayer: the answer is the same regardless of the number of players. question: Ada controls [Ethersworn Canonist]. They want to suspend [Shade of Trokair] and then cast [Divination]. Can they?

Ethersworn Canonist says "Each player who has cast a nonartifact spell this turn can't cast additional nonartifact spells." So:

Ada pays the suspend cost {W} and exiles Shade of Trokair with three time counters [702.62a].

3. Then Divination ({2}{U}, a sorcery) is Ada's first nonartifact spell cast this turn, so Ethersworn Canonist doesn't stop it [Ethersworn Canonist ruling #0]. After Divination resolves, however, Ada can't cast further nonartifact spells this turn.

Order assumption: I'm reading this as suspend first, then Divination, as asked. If Ada instead cast Divination first, Ethersworn Canonist would then prohibit casting Shade of Trokair, and so Ada could no longer take the suspend special action — the order genuinely matters here.

Ethersworn Canonist applies per player ("each player"), so this analysis is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table: each opponent independently gets one nonartifact spell per turn.

Later, when Shade of Trokair's last time counter is removed, the third suspend ability lets Ada cast it without paying its mana cost, ignoring timing restrictions [702.62a] [Shade of Trokair ruling #5]. That cast is a nonartifact spell, so Ethersworn Canonist can block it if Ada has already cast a nonartifact spell that turn; if Ada declines or can't cast it, it stays exiled.

question: Amia controls [Sanctuary Cat], and Nico controls [Glacial Chasm] and [Ral Zarek]. Amia attacks Ral Zarek with Sanctuary Cat. Is damage to Ral Zarek prevented?

Any +1/+1 counters or pump effects would then apply on top in layer 7c; here there are none, so it's 4/4.

Assumption on devotion: you gave devotion to white as 2; devotion to red and white together is presumably still less than seven (Iroas, God of Victory's own {R}{W} contributes 2, and Starfield of Nyx's {W} contributes 1). question: Amirah controls [Divine Visitation] and [Legion Warboss]. What are the characteristics of the token after Legion Warboss's trigger has resolved? Does it have to attack this combat?
gold:
A 4/4 Angel with flying, vigilance and haste. It is required to attack this combat if able. 

Divine Visitation creates a replacement effect that replaces Legion Warboss's token with a different token. After it's created as a 4/4 Angel, it gains haste and an effect is created that requires it to attack.
opus_answer:
Amirah gets a single 4/4 white Angel creature token with flying and vigilance instead of the 1/1 red Goblin token, and yes — that Angel token gains haste until end of turn and must attack this combat if able.

Why: Legion Warboss's beginning-of-combat trigger instructs Amirah to create a 1/1 red Goblin creature token. Divine Visitation is a replacement effect that applies to the creation of the token (rule 701.7b: replacement effects on token creation apply before continuous effects that would modify the token's characteristics), so the token is created as a 4/4 white Angel with flying and vigilance instead. Per [Divine Visitation ruling #2], the token's characteristics are entirely replaced — it has no abilities the original Goblin token would have had (the Goblin token had none anyway) — but anything else specified by the effect creating the token still applies. Legion Warboss's clause "That token gains haste until end of turn and attacks this combat if able" is exactly such an extra instruction, so it still applies to the Angel token.

So the Angel token has haste and is required to attack this combat if able. Note the "if able" limit: per [Legion Warboss ruling #2], if the token can't attack (for example, it becomes tapped), it simply doesn't, and if some cost is associated with attacking, Amirah isn't forced to pay it. The Angel token has vigilance, so attacking with it won't tap it.

The token is created untapped and not attacking — Legion Warboss's trigger doesn't put it onto the battlefield attacking, so Amirah declares it as an attacker normally in the declare attackers step. In a multiplayer game this is unchanged: Amirah chooses which defending player, planeswalker, or battle it attacks when attackers are declared; the requirement is only that it attack, not whom it attacks.

question: Nylah controls [Thorn of Amethyst] and [Chalice of the Void] with one charge counter on it. Ayden casts [Shivan Fire], paying the additional {1} for Thorn of Amethyst. Will Chalice of the Void trigger?
gold: Yes. The mana value of a card is derived from what's printed in the upper right-hand corner of the card. The mana value of Shivan Fire is 1, regardless of how much Ayden spent to cast it.

Yes — Chalice of the Void triggers and counters Shivan Fire.

Chalice of the Void checks the spell's mana value, not what was actually paid. Shivan Fire's mana cost is {R}, so its mana value is 1, matching the one charge counter. Thorn of Amethyst's "Noncreature spells cost {1} more to cast" only raises what Ayden must pay: the total cost becomes {R} plus {1} generic (and if Ayden also paid the kicker, an extra {4} generic). Cost increases and additional costs don't change the spell's mana cost — anything that asks for the mana cost still sees the original {R} (rules 118.8, 118.8d, 202.4, 601.2f).

So Chalice of the Void's triggered ability triggers on the cast and counters Shivan Fire. This works the same with two players or more than two: Chalice of the Void's ability watches "a player" casting a spell, so Nylah's Chalice of the Void triggers on any player's Shivan Fire.

question: Ariella casts [Unlicensed Disintegration], targeting their [Phyrexian Walker], which is their only artifact. Is Ariella dealt any damage?

- If Phyrexian Walker had become an illegal target before Unlicensed Disintegration resolved, the spell wouldn't resolve at all and no damage would be dealt to anyone [608.2b], [Unlicensed Disintegration ruling #0].

question: Avianna owns a [Dread] in exile as well as a [Yixlid Jailer] on the battlefield. Niko puts the Dread into the graveyard with [Ruin Processor]'s ability. Does Dread trigger?
gold: No. Triggered abilities are checked to see if they trigger immediately after the event occurs. Dread does not have any abilities at that time.
opus_answer:
No — Dread does not trigger, and it stays in Avianna's graveyard.

Why: Dread's ability reads "When Dread is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner's library." Because it triggers on being put into a graveyard "from anywhere" (here, from exile), it is not a leaves-the-battlefield ability and does not "look back in time" — it must trigger from the graveyard itself [603.6c] [603.10a] [Dread ruling #1] [Dread ruling #2]. Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," so the moment Dread arrives in the graveyard it has no abilities at all, and there is nothing there to trigger [Yixlid Jailer ruling #4] [Dread ruling #0].

A couple of related points:
- If instead some replacement effect had sent Dread somewhere other than the graveyard, the ability likewise wouldn't trigger, because it never would have been put into a graveyard [Dread ruling #3] [Yixlid Jailer ruling #5].
- Had the trigger actually occurred (no Yixlid Jailer) and Dread then left the graveyard before resolution, Avianna would still shuffle her library, but Dread would stay in its new zone [701.24c] [Dread ruling #3].
- Ruin Processor's ability moves Dread from exile to its owner's graveyard, so it is Avianna's graveyard even though Niko controls the trigger [Ruin Processor ruling #3].

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; Yixlid Jailer affects cards in every graveyard, and nothing here depends on player count.

Explanation and definitions
- A “zone-change trigger” is a triggered ability that triggers when an object changes zones (for example, an ability that triggers when an object is put into a graveyard). The game determines where such an ability triggers from according to the specific wording of the ability [603.6].
- Dread’s ability triggers “when [it is] put into a graveyard from anywhere,” so that triggered ability would trigger from the graveyard when Dread is moved there [Dread ruling #2].

Because Niko’s Ruin Processor ability put Dread from exile into Avianna’s graveyard, that is exactly the “from anywhere” event Dread’s ability cares about, but Yixlid Jailer prevents such a graveyard-triggering ability from triggering, so no trigger is created.
